projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Debbor Huntington was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Today is Tuesday, March the 18th, 2003, and this is the beginning of an interview with Veteran Debbor Richard Huntington at the V. A. Chicago Healthcare Facility, Lakeside Medical Center, at [address redacted], where he's a volunteer. Debbor is 76 years old, having been born on February the 24th, 1927. He presently resides at [address redacted]. My name is Ellen George, and I'm also a volunteer at Lakeside Medical Center, and I'll be the interviewer. Debbor, could you state for the recording what war, era, and branch of service you served in, and what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: I was a World War II, Navy Reserve, which changed to Navy, regular Navy, when the war broke out from '44 through '56; ten years enlistment with two years active and eight years in the inactive reserves. During that time I went to aviation ordinance school, gunnery school, radar school and operations in _______ Florida. I took my ordinance training in Norman, Oklahoma, and my gunnery training in Yellow Water, Oklahoma and in Jacksonville. The war broke out, and I was supposed to be shipped to an aircraft carrier. I had four days on the roster-- the roster before I was to be shipped over to the Pacific Coast for duty fighting the Japanese Betties, but they dropped the bomb, and they broke up our outfit during which time I spent some time as a _____ guard for the Navy base, and then they sent me over to Great Lakes Naval Training Center where I served as a blood runner in a van, and then a blood truck. Drove a red truck for a while, and then I was transferred to the office as a clerk separating the officers from the naval duties, figuring out their guide pay, their vacation pay, and pension pay. I enjoyed the service very much. I had a choice to transfer over to another enlistment, but I decided to go on to college, and so I took my discharge, my honorable discharge. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now, you say you served in World War II. Now, did you ever see any combat? Were you every really involved in combat?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: I'm not allowed to go into that.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Oh, okay, whatever. Do you have any really memorable experiences? (Telephone ringing.)

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Well I had two almost failed jumps from a parachute. I made two nearly fatal parachute jumps. In once case my leg was broken. In another case, I landed in a bunch of tall trees and broke several branches before I was finally stopped by one big branch. I woke up a couple of hours later and it was dark. Hanging by a parachute cord, I cut myself loose with a knife I, I had tucked away in my pocket and shimmied down the tree. When I landed I--I really smashed my leg up bad. I was in the infirmary, a make to -- makeshift infirmary where they put all the injured there, veterans for all services, in a ______ for about 2 weeks in intensive care. That's when I healed up and then went back to my duties.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now what were your duties at that time?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Oh, I was in operations, and we were actually flying the planes, shooting at dummy targets, and assembling and trouble shooting the guns and the other equipment aboard planes, loading bomb racks, etc.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now for all this which you have done, did you ever receive any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Well, I received a medal for being outside the territorial limits over the Atlantic Ocean, and the other regular medals for being in the war. Also, the sharp shooters' medal for sharp shooting ______.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: During this time, how did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: I stayed in touch with my folks by writing letters. My girlfriend too.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Well, how was the food like at that time?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: The food was pretty, pretty good. Once in a while they had a little skirmish in the P.X. or in the chow hall, but that was caused by younger people just coming in the service, not having a very good background in the military; they were just training. But I enjoyed the food. I always had a good appetite.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now, did you have plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Al--always. I had plenty of good supplies. Yah.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: During this time, did you ever feel pressure or stress on the job?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Well, about 2 o'clock in the morning one morning, a bunch of officers came in the barracks looking for a volunteer to fly over to the Bahara Islands, and the plane that flew over ran into some unfortunate circumstances and went down in the _____. I -- I missed going on that plane with a flip of the coin. The other guy won the flip and I lost. So--

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: And he's the one that went down?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: And he went down. His name was Anderson, and his father was a furniture salesman from what I understand.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Um-hum. A nice guy. Nice kid.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: What did you think of your fellow officers and soldiers?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Well my fellow officers were real buddies and real helpful to me at all times. I ran into -- we had a party one day and a couple of officers got a little rowdy drinking too much beer, but that was forgotten about, but as a rule in general they were all very good officers.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Do you recall the date of your service ended?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: My service ended August 28th, 1946, from active, and I was then considered to be in the reserves from August 28 to two years later -- I mean eight years later in the inactive reserves. When I was civilian-like, my boss wouldn't let me attend the meetings, which was unfortunate, so I was unable to be an active member, and I regret it.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: What did you do the days and weeks afterwards? Did you back to work? Go back to school?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: I obtained a job at a few factories. I worked in an electric outfit for a while, and then I worked at a factory making cables, riveting cables ____ then I attended the University of Illinois.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: And then I transferred over to Northern Illinois Teacher's College which was out in Northern Illinois University where I completed my degree in zoology and P.E.--minored in physical education.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: I made a -- about two or three close friendships.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: And you still keep in touch with them?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Well, these follows have all passed away now, unfortunately.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now, did you join a specific veterans' organization?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: I belonged to several air patrol, and I belonged to federal radio organizations where they send me radio communication papers every month or so where they would answer any questions I would have pertaining to radio.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now, did your military experience influence your thinking about the war or the military in general?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Oh, war is so complicated, so fierce, and so evil and so, you don't think about dying. As a matter of fact, I never expected to come back alive when I went in because of the way -- the attitude the Japanese had. I figured I best match their attitude, otherwise I would chicken out. I had a chance to chicken out, but I didn't. I stayed with it. I figured I was protecting my country. They were dropping bombs on us direct, directly on our heads, and I feel that God will _______.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now how did your service and the experiences affect your life?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: It, it showed me a lot of truths about people. What they are, what they think they are, and what they would like to be, what they should be, and what they really are. They showed me the difference, and I find this true about all people. We all have our faults, we all have our weaknesses, and we all have to fight the temptations of the wrong way to lead a good life.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Now, is there anything you would like to add that we have not covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: I would like to see the veterans taken better care of. In all ways.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: And that means hospitalization?

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: _______ hospitalization. It was promised to us. We were promised a house, and two cars, and a garage, and all our injuries would be taken care of, but this is not always the case.

sp.speaker: Ellen George
sp.p: Debbor, I want to thank you very much for taking the time and sharing some of your experiences with us. We truly, really appreciate it from the bottom of our hearts.

sp.speaker: Debbor Huntington
sp.p: Thank you.
